source.title: Scaling Behavior for Large Language Models regarding Numeral Systems: An Example using Pythia
source.authors: Zhejian Zhou; Jiayu Wang; Da-Hua Lin; Kai Chen

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests arithmetic-task performance across training-data scales and model sizes, rather than fitting language-model held-out-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly says it does not aim to predict performance when compute is scaled up and avoids fitting a scaling law. Its reported results compare arithmetic-task performance across numeral systems, data scales, model sizes, and training modes. Individual plotted datapoints are not numerically transcribed here; rows record the paper's explicit aggregate descriptions.
record.test_reason: The paper uses 'scaling behaviour' only as a proxy to compare numeral systems (base 10 vs 100 vs 1000) on synthetic arithmetic. It states it does not aim to predict performance with scale and deliberately fits no law (Sec. 2, App. C). It measures no held-out pretraining loss, fits no power law, does no extrapolation and no compute allocation. Its data-scale axis is task-specific training data, not pretraining scale. Its main results are between-tokenization comparisons, not tests of whether performance scales predictably. The few remarks on model size and saturation are unquantified asides about a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that base 10 is consistently more data-efficient than base 100/1000 across data scales and model sizes when trained from scratch, while fine-tuned models perform similarly, which they attribute to higher token frequencies. They also report extrapolation patterns (truncated addition, base-10 carry, token-level failures for larger bases). They explicitly avoid scaling-law prediction.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fitting held-out pretraining-loss curves, the study trains models on synthetic addition and multiplication data and compares arithmetic metrics across numeral systems, data scales, model sizes, and training modes.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with numeral system, arithmetic operation, from-scratch versus fine-tuning, training-data scale, and model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Arithmetic accuracy after task training on Pythia 70M–12B reportedly does not improve significantly with model size; smaller models were hard to train. This is unquantified and confounded by size-dependent learning rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-specific arithmetic performance (from scratch or fine-tuned Pythia) improves with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Addition accuracy saturates near 100% as synthetic training data grows from 2^13 to 2^19. Multiplication does not saturate, and base 10 gains more at large data scales.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task accuracy on synthetic arithmetic follows a smooth scaling curve in task-training data.

fits_no_version.finding: Base 10 tokenization is more data-efficient than base 100/1000 when training from scratch. The gap does not shrink with model size, and it is roughly on par under fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tokenization/numeral system shifts data-efficiency curves for arithmetic tasks.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: No power-law fitting or predictive evaluation is performed. The authors report limited hyperparameter grid search and instability in some training results; many outcome values appear in plots rather than tables.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted values and separate model-size/data-scale traces were not transcribed as separate rows; the paper's aggregate textual findings are recorded instead. Detailed plotted results are in Figures 2–4 and 9–10.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, data or compute.
No fits on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.
No depth/width variation at fixed parameter count.
No power-law form tested for fine-tuning or synthetic task training; authors say a law is hard to fit because addition saturates.
No relation of downstream performance to pretraining scale or loss, and no predictive test.
No comparison of fitted exponents or of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'tests' and 'supports' labels are not justified. The V6 rows measure tokenization differences, not predictable improvement with scale. The data-scale axis is synthetic task-training data rather than pretraining. The authors disclaim scaling-law aims and fit nothing. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fit loss power laws in parameter count, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit power laws on smaller runs or test prediction of larger-run losses.
It does not search for a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or fit its dependence on compute.
It compares Pythia model sizes, not architecture details such as depth and width at a fixed parameter count.
The study concerns synthetic arithmetic tasks and fine-tuning, but does not test whether the claimed loss power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.

It examines arithmetic-task performance against synthetic task-data scale and model size; it does not relate downstream performance to pretraining loss or test a predictive mapping from pretraining loss.
It does not compare fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal splits across setups. Its arithmetic-task saturation and setup differences are not tests of fitted loss-law dependence.

rows.value: Base 10 is consistently more data-efficient; the paper describes it as at least a constant magnitude more data-efficient.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative report across the listed Pythia sizes; the paper reports that the advantage does not diminish as model size increases.
rows.check: Compares base 10 vs base 100/1000 data efficiency on task-trained arithmetic. This is a numeral-system contrast, not a measure of predictable improvement with pretraining scale or loss, so it does not bear on V6. The state 'partial' has no referent.

rows.subject: Pythia models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared arithmetic-task performance across model sizes.
rows.value: The authors report that performance does not improve significantly with model size; the 70M and 410M models were particularly hard to train.
rows.note: This is the authors' aggregate statement; the paper does not give a fitted model-size scaling relationship.
rows.check: This is a one-sentence aside in App. C with no numbers, about accuracy on arithmetic trained directly on the task. It is confounded by different learning rates for 70M/410M (2e-4) vs larger models (2e-5) and by admitted training instability. It is not pretraining loss and not a downstream-vs-pretraining-scale mapping, so state is not readable as 'absent' for V6.

rows.subject: Pythia models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Examined arithmetic-task performance as training data increased.
rows.value: The paper reports a saturation trend for addition as more training data is used.
rows.note: This is a qualitative saturation report, not a fit or test of a held-out-loss power law.
rows.check: Saturation of a bounded accuracy metric on an easy task, as task-training data grows. It is not a loss curve and not a test of any version. Size is 'not stated' but Figure 2 covers all five Pythia sizes.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Arithmetic tasks across synthetic training-data scales, especially base-10 settings
reader_labels.reason: The study reports data-scale-dependent arithmetic performance and higher data efficiency for base 10 in R1–R8, but does not establish a predictive scaling relation.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Model-size scaling and addition at larger data scales
reader_labels.reason: Performance reportedly does not improve significantly with model size, and addition saturates with more data (R9–R10); the study does not fit a predictive performance law.
